claim: The bacterial flagellar motor is a cell-envelope-embedded macromolecular machine that functions as a cellular propeller.
source: The bacterial flagellar motor, a cell-envelope-embedded macromolecular machine that functions as a cellular propeller, exhibits significant structural variability between species.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial flagellar motors.

claim: The bacterial flagellar motor exhibits significant structural variability between species.
source: The bacterial flagellar motor, a cell-envelope-embedded macromolecular machine that functions as a cellular propeller, exhibits significant structural variability between species.
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging results presented in the manuscript showing different motor structures across species.

claim: Different torque-generating stator modules allow motors to operate in different pH, salt or viscosity levels.
source: Different torque-generating stator modules allow motors to operate in different pH, salt or viscosity levels.
evidence: This is supported by references to previous studies and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Motors with a single H+-driven stator have only the core periplasmic P- and L-rings.
source: Motors with a single H+-driven stator have only the core periplasmic P- and L-rings; those with dual H+-driven stators have an elaborated P-ring; and motors with Na+ or Na+/H+-driven stators have both their P- and L-rings embellished.
evidence: This is supported by ECT imaging data and bioinformatics analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Motors with dual H+-driven stators have an elaborated P-ring.
source: Motors with a single H+-driven stator have only the core periplasmic P- and L-rings; those with dual H+-driven stators have an elaborated P-ring; and motors with Na+ or Na+/H+-driven stators have both their P- and L-rings embellished.
evidence: This is supported by ECT imaging data of P. aeruginosa and L. pneumophila motors.

claim: Motors with Na+ or Na+/H+-driven stators have both their P- and L-rings embellished.
source: Motors with a single H+-driven stator have only the core periplasmic P- and L-rings; those with dual H+-driven stators have an elaborated P-ring; and motors with Na+ or Na+/H+-driven stators have both their P- and L-rings embellished.
evidence: This is supported by ECT imaging data of S. oneidensis and Vibrio species motors.

claim: The bacterial flagellum transforms the movement of ions (H+, Na+ or other cations) across the cell membrane into a mechanical torque to move the bacterial cell through its environment.
source: The bacterial flagellum is a macromolecular machine that transforms the movement of ions (H+, Na+ or other cations) across the cell membrane into a mechanical torque to move the bacterial cell through its environment (Ito and Takahashi, 2017; Sowa and Berry, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The flagellum consists of a cell-envelope-embedded motor, a hook which acts as a universal joint and a long propeller-like filament.
source: In general, the flagellum consists of a cell-envelope-embedded motor, a hook which acts as a universal joint and a long propeller-like filament (Berg, 2003; Erhardt et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The motor is composed of a rotor and a stator.
source: The motor is composed of a rotor and a stator: while the stator is the part of the motor that remains static, the rotor is the part that rotates and can rotate the filament in either a counterclockwise or clockwise direction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial flagellar motor structure.

claim: The stator is the part of the motor that remains static.
source: The motor is composed of a rotor and a stator: while the stator is the part of the motor that remains static, the rotor is the part that rotates and can rotate the filament in either a counterclockwise or clockwise direction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial flagellar motor function.

claim: The rotor is the part that rotates and can rotate the filament in either a counterclockwise or clockwise direction.
source: The motor is composed of a rotor and a stator: while the stator is the part of the motor that remains static, the rotor is the part that rotates and can rotate the filament in either a counterclockwise or clockwise direction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial flagellar motor function.

claim: The Shewanella putrefaciens flagellum can wrap around the cell to mediate a screw-like motion that allows the cell to escape narrow traps.
source: it was recently reported that the Shewanella putrefaciens flagellum can wrap around the cell to mediate a screw-like motion that allows the cell to escape narrow traps (Kühn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Bacterial flagella participate in biofilm formation.
source: Besides their role in motility, bacterial flagella participate in other vital activities of the cell such as biofilm formation (Belas, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The virulence of many human pathogens depends directly on their flagella.
source: Moreover, the virulence of many human pathogens depends directly on their flagella, with flagellated strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Legionella pneumophila causing more serious infections with higher mortality rates (Appelt and Heuner, 2017; Feldman et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Flagellated strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Legionella pneumophila cause more serious infections with higher mortality rates.
source: Moreover, the virulence of many human pathogens depends directly on their flagella, with flagellated strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Legionella pneumophila causing more serious infections with higher mortality rates (Appelt and Heuner, 2017; Feldman et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: P. aeruginosa lacking fully-assembled flagella cause no mortality.
source: P. aeruginosa lacking fully-assembled flagella cause no mortality and are 75% less likely to cause pneumonia in mice (Feldman et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: P. aeruginosa lacking fully-assembled flagella are 75% less likely to cause pneumonia in mice.
source: P. aeruginosa lacking fully-assembled flagella cause no mortality and are 75% less likely to cause pneumonia in mice (Feldman et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The best-studied flagellar motor is in Salmonella enterica.
source: The best-studied flagellar motor, in Salmonella enterica, consists of several sub-complexes, which we will describe in order from the inside out.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The MS ring is formed by the protein FliF.
source: On the cytoplasmic side are the inner-membrane-embedded MS ring (formed by the protein FliF) and the C-ring (aka the switch complex, formed by FliN, FliM and FliG).
evidence: This is established knowledge about flagellar motor structure.

claim: The C-ring is formed by FliN, FliM and FliG.
source: On the cytoplasmic side are the inner-membrane-embedded MS ring (formed by the protein FliF) and the C-ring (aka the switch complex, formed by FliN, FliM and FliG).
evidence: This is established knowledge about flagellar motor structure.

claim: The stator complex has 4:2 stoichiometry of MotA and MotB.
source: Spanning the space from the inner membrane to the peptidoglycan cell wall is the ion channel (called the stator), a complex of two proteins (MotA and MotB) with 4:2 stoichiometry (Koebnik, 1995; Kojima, 2015; Morimoto and Minamino, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The stator complex is anchored to the peptidoglycan.
source: This complex is anchored to the peptidoglycan and converts the flux of ions across the bacterial membrane into a torque through the interaction of the so-called 'torque-helix' in MotA with FliG in the C-ring.
evidence: This is established knowledge about flagellar motor function.

claim: The stator complex converts the flux of ions across the bacterial membrane into a torque through the interaction of the 'torque-helix' in MotA with FliG in the C-ring.
source: This complex is anchored to the peptidoglycan and converts the flux of ions across the bacterial membrane into a torque through the interaction of the so-called 'torque-helix' in MotA with FliG in the C-ring.
evidence: This is established knowledge about flagellar motor function.

claim: Extra periplasmic rings were found to elaborate the canonical P- and L-rings in the motor of the Gammaproteobacteria Vibrio species.
source: For example, extra periplasmic rings were found to elaborate the canonical P- and L-rings in the motor of the Gammaproteobacteria Vibrio species.
evidence: This is supported by references to previous studies.

claim: The extra periplasmic rings in Vibrio species are called the T-ring (MotX and Y) and H-ring (FlgO, P and T).
source: These rings are called the T-ring (MotX and Y) and H-ring (FlgO, P and T) (Terashima et al., 2010; Terashima et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The motors of Vibrio and other marine bacteria employ different stators (PomA and PomB) which utilize Na+.
source: Unlike the S. enterica motor described above, which is driven by H+ ions, the motors of Vibrio and other marine bacteria employ different stators (PomA and PomB) which utilize Na+.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Vibrio flagellar motors.

claim: Na+-dependent stators generate higher torque (~2200 pN) than H+-dependent stators (~1200 pN).
source: These Na+-dependent stators generate higher torque (~2200 pN) than H+-dependent stators (~1200 pN), driving the motor at higher speeds (up to 1,700 Hz compared to ~300 Hz in H+-driven motors) (Magariyama et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Na+-dependent stators drive the motor at higher speeds (up to 1,700 Hz compared to ~300 Hz in H+-driven motors).
source: These Na+-dependent stators generate higher torque (~2200 pN) than H+-dependent stators (~1200 pN), driving the motor at higher speeds (up to 1,700 Hz compared to ~300 Hz in H+-driven motors) (Magariyama et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The single stator system of Bacillus clausii KSM-K16 is able to use both Na+ and H+ at different pH levels.
source: Interestingly, it has also been shown that the single stator system of Bacillus clausii KSM-K16 is able to use both Na+ and H+ at different pH levels (Terahara et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Vibrio alginolyticus uses two distinct types of motors to move in different environments: a polar Na+-driven flagellum and lateral H+-driven flagella.
source: Some species, however, such as Vibrio alginolyticus, use two distinct types of motors to move in different environments: a polar Na+-driven flagellum and lateral H+-driven flagella.
evidence: This is established knowledge about V. alginolyticus motility.

claim: P. aeruginosa employs a dual H+-driven stator system (MotAB and MotCD).
source: For example, P. aeruginosa employs a dual H+-driven stator system (MotAB and MotCD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. aeruginosa flagellar motor.

claim: The MotAB system is sufficient to move P. aeruginosa cells in a liquid environment.
source: While the MotAB system is sufficient to move the cell in a liquid environment (Doyle et al., 2004), MotCD is necessary to allow the cell to move in more viscous conditions (Toutain et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: MotCD is necessary to allow P. aeruginosa cells to move in more viscous conditions.
source: While the MotAB system is sufficient to move the cell in a liquid environment (Doyle et al., 2004), MotCD is necessary to allow the cell to move in more viscous conditions (Toutain et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 combines both Na+- and H+-dependent stators in a single motor.
source: Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 combines both Na+- and H+-dependent stators in a single motor, enabling the bacterium to move efficiently under conditions of different pH and Na+ concentration (Paulick et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The dual stator system in S. oneidensis MR-1 enables the bacterium to move efficiently under conditions of different pH and Na+ concentration.
source: Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 combines both Na+- and H+-dependent stators in a single motor, enabling the bacterium to move efficiently under conditions of different pH and Na+ concentration (Paulick et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The three motors (L. pneumophila, P. aeruginosa, and S. oneidensis) shared the conserved core structure of the flagellar motor.
source: Although the three motors shared the conserved core structure of the flagellar motor, they exhibited different periplasmic decorations surrounding this conserved core.
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The three motors (L. pneumophila, P. aeruginosa, and S. oneidensis) exhibited different periplasmic decorations surrounding the conserved core.
source: Although the three motors shared the conserved core structure of the flagellar motor, they exhibited different periplasmic decorations surrounding this conserved core.
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The S. oneidensis and P. aeruginosa averages showed clear densities corresponding to the stators.
source: While the S. oneidensis and P. aeruginosa averages showed clear densities corresponding to the stators (Figure 1E,F,K and L, dark orange density), none were visible in the L. pneumophila average, suggesting that they were more variable, or dynamic and therefore are not visible in the average (see e.g., (Chen et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2017)).
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: No stator densities were visible in the L. pneumophila average, suggesting that they were more variable, or dynamic.
source: While the S. oneidensis and P. aeruginosa averages showed clear densities corresponding to the stators (Figure 1E,F,K and L, dark orange density), none were visible in the L. pneumophila average, suggesting that they were more variable, or dynamic and therefore are not visible in the average (see e.g., (Chen et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2017)).
evidence: This is an inference based on the ECT imaging data and supported by citations to previous studies showing similar phenomena.

claim: An extra ring outside the outer membrane was observed in the S. oneidensis motor.
source: Interestingly, we observed a novel feature in the S. oneidensis motor: an extra ring outside the outer membrane (Figure 1A–F, purple density).
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In some tomograms two extracellular rings appeared to be present in S. oneidensis.
source: Although in some tomograms two extracellular rings appeared to be present (see Figure 1A and C), only one ring was visible in the sub-tomogram average which could be either because one of the rings is more dynamic or substoichiometric (Figure 1B,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for more examples of single motors).
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Only one extracellular ring was visible in the S. oneidensis sub-tomogram average.
source: Although in some tomograms two extracellular rings appeared to be present (see Figure 1A and C), only one ring was visible in the sub-tomogram average which could be either because one of the rings is more dynamic or substoichiometric (Figure 1B,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for more examples of single motors).
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The extracellular ring in S. oneidensis is reminiscent of the O-ring described in the sheathed flagellum of Vibrio alginolyticus.
source: This structure is reminiscent of the O-ring (outer membrane ring) described recently in the sheathed flagellum of Vibrio alginolyticus (Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarity and supported by a citation.

claim: The V. alginolyticus O-ring was associated with a 90° bend in the outer membrane.
source: However, while the V. alginolyticus O-ring was associated with a 90° bend in the outer membrane, no such outer membrane bend was seen in the unsheathed S. oneidensis flagellum, so the function of this structure remains mysterious.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: No outer membrane bend was seen in the unsheathed S. oneidensis flagellum.
source: However, while the V. alginolyticus O-ring was associated with a 90° bend in the outer membrane, no such outer membrane bend was seen in the unsheathed S. oneidensis flagellum, so the function of this structure remains mysterious.
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data.

claim: The most striking difference between the three motor structures was the L- and P-rings, which were highly elaborated in S. oneidensis.
source: The most striking difference between the three motor structures was the L- and P-rings, which were highly elaborated in S. oneidensis.
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The P. aeruginosa and L. pneumophila motors lacked additional rings associated with the L-ring.
source: The P. aeruginosa and L. pneumophila motors lacked additional rings associated with the L-ring, but showed smaller elaborations of their P-rings.
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The P. aeruginosa and L. pneumophila motors showed smaller elaborations of their P-rings.
source: The P. aeruginosa and L. pneumophila motors lacked additional rings associated with the L-ring, but showed smaller elaborations of their P-rings.
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Motors with similar stator type share similar structural characteristics.
source: Interestingly, we found that motors with similar stator type also shared similar structural characteristics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of ECT structures and bioinformatics analysis.

claim: Motors with a single H+-dependent stator system did not show any periplasmic elaborations beyond the conserved flagellar core.
source: While the two motors with a single H+-dependent stator system did not show any periplasmic elaborations beyond the conserved flagellar core, the dual H+-dependent stator systems had an extra ring surrounding their P-ring, with no embellishment of the L-ring.
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: The dual H+-dependent stator systems had an extra ring surrounding their P-ring, with no embellishment of the L-ring.
source: While the two motors with a single H+-dependent stator system did not show any periplasmic elaborations beyond the conserved flagellar core, the dual H+-dependent stator systems had an extra ring surrounding their P-ring, with no embellishment of the L-ring.
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data of P. aeruginosa and L. pneumophila.

claim: The Na+-dependent motors of the Vibrio spp., together with the Na+-H+-dependent motor of S. oneidensis, have extra components surrounding both their P- and L- rings.
source: The Na+-dependent motors of the Vibrio spp., together with the Na+-H+-dependent motor of S. oneidensis, have extra components surrounding both their P- and L- rings.
evidence: This is supported by the ECT imaging data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: In Vibrio, the extra periplasmic rings are known as the T-ring (surrounding the P- ring and formed by the MotX and MotY proteins) and the H-ring (surrounding the L-ring and consisting of the FlgO, FlgP and FlgT proteins).
source: In Vibrio, these extra periplasmic rings are known as the T-ring (surrounding the P- ring and formed by the MotX and MotY proteins) and the H-ring (surrounding the L-ring and consisting of the FlgO, FlgP and FlgT proteins).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Vibrio flagellar motor structure.

claim: The presence of the T- and H-rings was suggested to be specific to the Na+-driven Vibrio motors.
source: The presence of the T- and H-rings was suggested to be specific to the Na+-driven Vibrio motors (Minamino and Imada, 2015) with the FlgT protein required for the formation of both rings (Terashima et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The FlgT protein is required for the formation of both T- and H-rings in Vibrio.
source: The presence of the T- and H-rings was suggested to be specific to the Na+-driven Vibrio motors (Minamino and Imada, 2015) with the FlgT protein required for the formation of both rings (Terashima et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: MotX and MotY are important for flagellar rotation in S. oneidensis.
source: Previous studies showed that MotX and MotY are important for flagellar rotation in S. oneidensis but it was not known whether they form part of the motor or not (Koerdt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: MotY is involved in the function of the P. aeruginosa motor.
source: Similarly, bioinformatics analysis and biochemical studies showed that MotY is involved in the function of the P. aeruginosa motor, but the structural basis of this role was not known (Doyle et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Candidates for all five proteins constituting the T- and H-rings were found in S. oneidensis.
source: While we found candidates for all five proteins constituting the T- and H-rings in S. oneidensis as previously suggested (Wu et al., 2011), only MotY candidates were found in L. pneumophila and P. aeruginosa (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis presented in the manuscript and a citation.

claim: Only MotY candidates were found in L. pneumophila and P. aeruginosa.
source: While we found candidates for all five proteins constituting the T- and H-rings in S. oneidensis as previously suggested (Wu et al., 2011), only MotY candidates were found in L. pneumophila and P. aeruginosa (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The bioinformatics findings are in accordance with the ECT structures showing that L. pneumophila and P. aeruginosa motors have a ring surrounding only their P-rings while the S. oneidensis motor has rings surrounding both the P- and L-rings.
source: This is in accordance with our ECT structures, which showed that L. pneumophila and P. aeruginosa motors have a ring surrounding only their P-rings while the S. oneidensis motor has rings surrounding both the P- and L-rings.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the bioinformatics data with the ECT imaging data.

claim: The rings in S. oneidensis are likely T- and H-rings, as in Vibrio.
source: These rings are likely T- and H-rings, respectively, as in Vibrio.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarity and bioinformatics analysis.

claim: The lack of candidate MotX homologs in the genomes of L. pneumophila and P. aeruginosa is consistent with their lack of PomB.
source: The lack of candidate MotX homologs in the genomes of L. pneumophila and P. aeruginosa (Table 1) is consistent with their lack of PomB, the component of the Na+-dependent stator with which MotX interacts.
evidence: This is an inference based on bioinformatics analysis and established knowledge about protein interactions.

claim: The absence of candidates for FlgT in the L. pneumophila and P. aeruginosa genomes suggests that it may not be required for the recruitment of MotY as in Vibrio species.
source: Interestingly, the absence of candidates for FlgT in the L. pneumophila and P. aeruginosa genomes suggests that it may not be required for the recruitment of MotY as in Vibrio species.
evidence: This is an inference based on bioinformatics analysis.

claim: In all species examined, motors with single H+-driven stator systems lacked homologs of H- or T-ring components.
source: In all species we examined, we observed the same pattern: (i) genomes of species with single H+-driven stator systems lacked homologs of H- or T-ring components; (ii) genomes of species with Na+ (or Na+-H+) stator systems contained homologs of all H- and T-ring components, and (iii) genomes of species with dual H+-driven stator systems contained candidate homologs only for the T-ring component MotY.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In all species examined, genomes of species with Na+ (or Na+-H+) stator systems contained homologs of all H- and T-ring components.
source: In all species we examined, we observed the same pattern: (i) genomes of species with single H+-driven stator systems lacked homologs of H- or T-ring components; (ii) genomes of species with Na+ (or Na+-H+) stator systems contained homologs of all H- and T-ring components, and (iii) genomes of species with dual H+-driven stator systems contained candidate homologs only for the T-ring component MotY.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In all species examined, genomes of species with dual H+-driven stator systems contained candidate homologs only for the T-ring component MotY.
source: In all species we examined, we observed the same pattern: (i) genomes of species with single H+-driven stator systems lacked homologs of H- or T-ring components; (ii) genomes of species with Na+ (or Na+-H+) stator systems contained homologs of all H- and T-ring components, and (iii) genomes of species with dual H+-driven stator systems contained candidate homologs only for the T-ring component MotY.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chromohalobacter salexigens DSM 3043 contained a homolog of FlgO in addition to MotY.
source: The sole exception to this rule was Chromohalobacter salexigens DSM 3043, which contained a homolog of FlgO in addition to MotY.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: None of the thirteen species with dual H+-driven stator systems examined contained a homolog of FlgT.
source: None of the thirteen species with dual H+-driven stator systems we examined contained a homolog of FlgT, further suggesting that it is not essential for MotY stabilization in this group.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: FlgT is not essential for MotY stabilization in species with dual H+-driven stator systems.
source: None of the thirteen species with dual H+-driven stator systems we examined contained a homolog of FlgT, further suggesting that it is not essential for MotY stabilization in this group.
evidence: This is an inference based on bioinformatics analysis.

claim: There is a correlation between the structural elaboration of the flagellar motor of Gammaproteobacteria and the type of its torque-generating unit, the stator.
source: Together, our results from ECT imaging of flagellar motors in situ and bioinformatics analysis reveal a correlation between the structural elaboration of the flagellar motor of Gammaproteobacteria and the type of its torque-generating unit, the stator (summarized in Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by ECT imaging data and bioinformatics analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Low-speed motors with single H+-stator systems have only the P- and L-rings.
source: Low-speed motors with single H+-stator systems have only the P- and L-rings, while high-speed motors using Na+ have two extra periplasmic rings, the T- and H-rings.
evidence: This is supported by ECT imaging data and bioinformatics analysis.

claim: High-speed motors using Na+ have two extra periplasmic rings, the T- and H-rings.
source: Low-speed motors with single H+-stator systems have only the P- and L-rings, while high-speed motors using Na+ have two extra periplasmic rings, the T- and H-rings.
evidence: This is supported by ECT imaging data and bioinformatics analysis.

claim: Motors with dual H+-driven stator systems represent a hybrid structure, elaborating their P-rings with MotY.
source: Unexpectedly, we find that motors with dual H+-driven stator systems represent a hybrid structure between the two, elaborating their P-rings with one of the five components of the T- and H-rings, MotY.
evidence: This is supported by ECT imaging data and bioinformatics analysis.

claim: The presence of extra elaborations in the motor is encoded in the genome and is not related to whether or not a stator subunit is recruited on the motor.
source: It is important to note that the presence of these extra elaborations in the motor is encoded in the genome and is not related to whether or not a stator subunit is recruited on the motor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the bioinformatics analysis showing genetic encoding of these components.

claim: The extra MotY ring might help to stabilize the motor under conditions of increased load, as in the viscous environment of the pulmonary system encountered by L. pneumophila and P. aeruginosa.
source: This extra MotY ring might help to stabilize the motor under conditions of increased load, as in the viscous environment of the pulmonary system encountered by L. pneumophila and P. aeruginosa.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural findings and the ecological niches of these bacteria.

claim: These pathogenic Gammaproteobacteria species could have borrowed a motor stabilization strategy from related Na+-driven motors to allow them to colonize animal hosts.
source: These results therefore suggest an evolutionary pathway in which these pathogenic Gammaproteobacteria species could have borrowed a motor stabilization strategy from related Na+-driven motors to allow them to colonize animal hosts.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary pathways based on the structural and bioinformatics findings.

claim: The resolution of the L. pneumophila motor structure is 6.4 nm at a 0.143 cutoff.
source: Resolutions at a 0.143 cutoff (dashed line) are: L. pneumophila, 6.4 nm; P. aeruginosa, 5.9 nm; S. oneidensis MR-1, 6.9 nm.
evidence: This is data from the resolution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The resolution of the P. aeruginosa motor structure is 5.9 nm at a 0.143 cutoff.
source: Resolutions at a 0.143 cutoff (dashed line) are: L. pneumophila, 6.4 nm; P. aeruginosa, 5.9 nm; S. oneidensis MR-1, 6.9 nm.
evidence: This is data from the resolution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The resolution of the S. oneidensis MR-1 motor structure is 6.9 nm at a 0.143 cutoff.
source: Resolutions at a 0.143 cutoff (dashed line) are: L. pneumophila, 6.4 nm; P. aeruginosa, 5.9 nm; S. oneidensis MR-1, 6.9 nm.
evidence: This is data from the resolution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The P. aeruginosa motor average was obtained by averaging 144 sub-volumes.
source: The averages were obtained by averaging 144 sub-volumes P. aeruginosa, 100 sub-volumes S. oneidensis MR-1 and 45 sub-volumes L. pneumophila.
evidence: This is methodological data about the sub-tomogram averaging process.

claim: The S. oneidensis MR-1 motor average was obtained by averaging 100 sub-volumes.
source: The averages were obtained by averaging 144 sub-volumes P. aeruginosa, 100 sub-volumes S. oneidensis MR-1 and 45 sub-volumes L. pneumophila.
evidence: This is methodological data about the sub-tomogram averaging process.

claim: The L. pneumophila motor average was obtained by averaging 45 sub-volumes.
source: The averages were obtained by averaging 144 sub-volumes P. aeruginosa, 100 sub-volumes S. oneidensis MR-1 and 45 sub-volumes L. pneumophila.
evidence: This is methodological data about the sub-tomogram averaging process.

claim: An E-value cutoff of <1×10−10 was used for the bioinformatics analysis.
source: An E-value cutoff of <1×10−10 was used.
evidence: This is methodological data about the bioinformatics analysis.
